abstract: The drug improved the ability to focus — but only in women. Plus, US climate scientists are facing a deluge of public-records requests and why a sleep-disorder drug might be the next big blockbuster.
journal: Nature
journal_ref: Nature
title: Daily Briefing: Tiny doses of LSD seem to boost cognition

abstract: BACKGROUND: Retatrutide, an investigational triple agonist of glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide, glucagon-like peptide 1, and glucagon receptors, may be useful for treating obstructive sleep apnea (OSA). METHODS: In two phase 3, double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trials nested within larger basket trials of once-weekly subcutaneous retatrutide, we assigned adults with moderate-to-severe OSA and a body-mass index (the weight in kilograms divided by the square of the height in meters) of at least 27, without (TRIUMPH-1-OSA) or with (TRIUMPH-2-OSA) type 2 diabetes, to receive retatrutide (4, 9, or 12 mg) or placebo. The primary end point was the change in the apnea-hypopnea index (AHI, the average number of apneas and hypopneas per hour of sleep) at 80 weeks with 9 mg and 12 mg of retatrutide. For OSA-related end points, a hybrid-treatment estimand was applied, with a hypothetical strategy used for participants who had intercurrent events suggesting treatment failure and a treatment-policy strategy used elsewhere. We also report intention-to-treat (ITT) results. RESULTS: A total of 243 participants underwent randomization in TRIUMPH-1-OSA and 448 in TRIUMPH-2-OSA. The baseline mean AHI was 58.6 and 55.9 events per hour, respectively, and the mean body weight was 119.6 and 115.9 kg. At 80 weeks, the mean changes in the AHI (hybrid-treatment estimand) with retatrutide in TRIUMPH-1-OSA were -22.9 (4 mg), -34.3 (9 mg), and -31.7 (12 mg) events per hour, versus -9.9 with placebo (difference vs. placebo, -13.0 [95% confidence interval {CI}, -23.0 to -3.0], -24.4 [95% CI, -34.1 to -14.7], and -21.9 [95% CI, -32.2 to -11.5], respectively). The changes with retatrutide in TRIUMPH-2-OSA were -19.2 (4 mg), -24.7 (9 mg), and -25.4 (12 mg) events per hour, versus -10.3 with placebo (difference vs. placebo, -8.9 [95% CI, -15.9 to -2.0], -14.4 [95% CI, -21.6 to -7.2], and -15.1 [95% CI, -22.5 to -7.7]). For the ITT estimand, the corresponding differences from placebo were -13.2 (95% CI, -22.6 to -3.9), -24.7 (95% CI, -34.1 to -15.3), and -22.5 (95% CI, -31.9 to -13.1) in TRIUMPH-1-OSA and -8.8 (95% CI, -15.8 to -1.7), -13.9 (95% CI, -21.3 to -6.6), and -15.0 (95% CI, -22.5 to -7.4) in TRIUMPH-2-OSA. The mean percent change in body weight with retatrutide (key secondary end point) was -12.5 to -22.2% in TRIUMPH-1-OSA and -12.1 to -18.5% in TRIUMPH-2-OSA, versus -4.8% and -5.6% with placebo (treatment-regimen estimand). The most common adverse events were gastrointestinal. CONCLUSIONS: In adults with OSA and obesity or overweight with or without type 2 diabetes, retatrutide resulted in significantly greater decreases in the AHI than placebo. (Funded by Eli Lilly; TRIUMPH-1 and -2 ClinicalTrials.gov numbers, NCT05929066 and NCT05929079.).
journal: New England Journal of Medicine
journal_ref: New England Journal of Medicine
title: Retatrutide Once Weekly for Treatment of Obstructive Sleep Apnea

abstract: Precise genome editing in hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) holds great potential for treating inherited blood disorders; however, low knock-in (KI) efficiency and loss of functional HSCs after genome editing remain major obstacles. Here, we demonstrate that transient inhibition of Ataxia-Telangiectasia Mutated (ATM) kinase markedly enhanced KI efficiency in mouse HSCs genome-edited with Cas9/ribonucleoprotein (RNP) and AAV donor DNA. Phosphoproteomic and capillary western blot analyses revealed that ATM inhibition suppressed aberrant Cas9-AAV-induced ATM activation and the subsequent DNA damage response, reduced p53-dependent apoptosis, and enhanced survival of KI HSCs. In serial transplantation assays, ATM inhibition preserved long-term engrafting KI HSCs, increasing their frequency from ~0.3 to 40% in secondary recipients, an over 100-fold improvement. Furthermore, in an X-linked severe combined immunodeficient mouse model, ATM inhibition increased KI efficiency and restored T- and B cell differentiation. Comprehensive safety analyses, including long-read nanopore sequencing, amplicon deep sequencing, whole genome sequencing and clonal tracking, did not detect increased genomic alterations, chromosomal abnormalities, or clonal expansion following transient ATM inhibition. Taken together, these findings establish transient ATM inhibition as an effective strategy to enhance KI-mediated genome editing while maintaining the long-term repopulating capacity of HSCs.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Transient ATM inhibition enhances knock-in efficiency in hematopoietic stem cells by attenuating the DNA damage response

abstract: Chromosome 3q (3q) amplification is a frequent event in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) and other cancer types, yet therapeutic strategies targeting oncogenic drivers within this amplicon have been unsuccessful. Our study revealed that the 3q amplicon encodes multiple Golgi-related proteins, including Phospholipase D1 (PLD1), which catalyzes the production of a potential oncogenic lipid, phosphatidic acid. We found that PLD1 is highly expressed in 3q-amplified NSCLC (3q-NSCLC) and its enzymatic activity is further boosted by coamplified PLD1 activator, ARF-like GTPase 14. High PLD1 activity is essential for 3q-NSCLC growth and metastasis. Mechanistically, PLD1 drives secretion of oncogenic factors via the carriers from the trans Golgi network to the cell surface pathway to support tumor growth. Transferrin receptor 1 (TFRC), which encodes a membrane protein, is coamplified with PLD1 and overexpressed in 3q-NSCLC. A TFRC antibody-drug conjugate (ADC) carrying a PLD1 inhibitor exhibited potential antitumor activity in mouse models. These findings establish PLD1 as a promoter of 3q-NSCLC and provide proof of concept for the development of PLD1-targeted therapies, including ADC-based approaches, for this challenging cancer subtype.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: PLD1-driven oncogenic secretion creates a therapeutic vulnerability in chromosome 3q–amplified NSCLC

abstract: The elemental composition of organisms links physiology to biogeochemical cycles, yet the relative contributions of evolutionary divergence, ecology, and allometry to stoichiometric variation remain incompletely resolved. Here, we integrate a global insect stoichiometric database spanning 223 species with a comprehensive phylogenetic backbone to evaluate the relative importance of hypothesized ecophysiological drivers of carbon (C), nitrogen (N), and phosphorus (P) stoichiometry within a multivariate framework. We found a strong phylogenetic signal in stoichiometric ratios and in P and N content, with evolutionary divergence (phylogenetic structure) accounting for approximately half of the explained variation in P-based ratios, exceeding the contribution of any individual ecological predictor. Phylogenetically corrected models recover trophic enrichment across successive trophic levels, consistent with previously documented patterns, and positive scaling between body mass and both C:P and N:P, in line with the general predictions of the Growth Rate Hypothesis. Temperature was the strongest ecological predictor of insect stoichiometry, with positive effects on C:P and N:P ratios and a negative effect on C:N, highlighting the thermal underpinnings of previously observed geographic patterns. Finally, our models recover higher P and lower C in terrestrial insects relative to their aquatic counterparts, contrary to classic expectations that invoke differences in structural constraints and autotrophic composition across habitats. Together, our work shows that variation in insect stoichiometry emerges from the interacting influences of evolutionary divergence and ecological and physiological variation, which can be disentangled through appropriately scaled, phylogenetically informed analyses.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Ecological, physiological, and evolutionary drivers of stoichiometry in insects

abstract: Respiratory infections remain a major global health challenge, further compounded by antibiotic resistance. Among these, mycoplasmal pneumonia represents a particularly prevalent and refractory form. Here, using targeted enzymatic fragmentation combined with multidimensional NMR analysis, we resolved the structure of a homogeneous Ganoderma lucidum polysaccharide, GLFP2, and identified β-(1→6)-linked galactosyl motifs as key structural features. Despite minimal systemic absorption, oral GLFP2 alleviated mycoplasmal pneumonia in mice. Instead, GLFP2 reshaped the gut microbiota and functionally reprogrammed gut microbiota-derived extracellular vesicles (GMEVs), whose transplantation alone was sufficient to confer pulmonary protection. Orally administered GMEVs remained bioactive, showed systemic exposure, associated with the lung, and were preferentially taken up by alveolar macrophages. These vesicles activated AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) signaling, suppressed the S100A8/A9 inflammatory axis, and limited neutrophil-driven immunopathology. Collectively, these findings identify microbiota-derived vesicles as effectors of gut–lung communication and use a defined polysaccharide to uncover a remote protective mechanism against pneumonia.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Gut microbiota vesicle reprogramming by Ganoderma lucidum polysaccharide alleviates mycoplasmal pneumonia via the gut–lung axis

abstract: Immune–neuron interactions play a critical role in neuroinflammatory and neurodegenerative diseases, such as Alzheimer’s disease (AD), but how CD8⁺ T cells contribute to brain pathology remains poorly understood. Amyloid-β (Aβ), a hallmark of AD, is known to trigger neuronal stress and inflammation. Here, we established a human cortical organoid (hCO) model to investigate CD8⁺ T cell responses to Aβ-induced neurodegenerative stress. Aβ exposure increased neuronal expression of CX3CL1 (fractalkine), which engages its receptor CX3CR1 on CD8⁺ T cells. Transwell migration assays showed enhanced recruitment of CX3CR1⁺ CD8⁺ T cells toward Aβ-treated hCOs. In parallel, Aβ upregulated IL-15 expression, a cytokine that supports CD8⁺ T cell activation. The infiltration of CD8⁺ T cells led to neuronal injury, marked by MAP2 loss and cleaved Caspase-3 activation, accompanied by an increase in gene signatures for cell death and inflammation. Exposure to the conditioned medium of activated CX3CR1 high CD8⁺ T cell recapitulated this damage, and the neutralization of CD8 + T cell cytokines and cytotoxic molecules rescued the phenotype. These findings identify the CX3CL1–CX3CR1 axis and CD8⁺ T cell effector programs as drivers of neurotoxicity and establish brain organoids as a platform to study immune-driven neurodegeneration.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: CX3CL1 (fractalkine)–CX3CR1 interface drives CD8⁺ T cell–induced neurodegeneration in human brain organoids

abstract: Most nonmammalian tetrapods exhibit more than three phalanges in their posterior digits (III–V), whereas mammals are restricted to no more than three. So far, the molecular mechanism underlying this evolutionary reduction and the functions of Lhx2 and Lhx9 in digit development remain unclear. Here we show divergent evolution of Lhx2 and Lhx9 expression patterns in embryonic limbs across tetrapods. We further demonstrate that although ectopic overexpression of each gene in chick embryos delayed limb skeletal development, only Lhx9 reduced the phalanx number in the posterior digits. Transcriptomic analysis showed that Lhx2 regulates pathways for chondrocyte and osteoblast differentiation, and Lhx9 preferentially influences skeletal segmentation via the bone morphogenetic protein (BMP) pathway. The unique function and differential expression of Lhx9 in the limb buds between mammals and nonmammalian tetrapods suggest it may have acquired a role in suppressing phalanx number, driving the evolutionary reduction of phalanx number in mammals.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Lhx9 specifically modulates phalanx number, whereas Lhx2 constrains digit length in tetrapods

abstract: Gap junctions are important regulators of the biology of neural stem cells. Both in vertebrates with regenerative abilities and neonatal rodents, ependymal cells communicate via connexin (Cx) 43 and Cx26. Gap junction coupling and Cx26 are down-regulated as the ependyma becomes quiescent in adulthood, but injury overrules this developmental down-regulation suggesting a role for Cx signaling in the reactivation of ependymal cells. However, direct evidence of the involvement of these Cxs in the reactivation of the ependymal stem cell niche is lacking. Here, we aim to explore the role of Cx26 and Cx43 in the response of ependymal cells to injury by means of specific genetic deletion. We find that Cx26 is critical for the proliferative response of ependymal cells to injury. The reduced response of ependymal cells by Cx26 deletion increased the extension of the lesion because of impaired healing resulting from a weak contribution of the ependymal stem cell niche. On the other hand, Cx43—via gap junction coupling and hemichannels—plays a key role in the communication of Ca 2+ signals between ependymal cells induced by activation of P2X7 receptors. Our data show that Cxs are relevant targets to manipulate the ependymal stem cell niche to achieve better healing after spinal cord injury.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Connexins are essential for the contribution of latent progenitors to healing after spinal cord injury

abstract: Suppression of transposable elements (TEs) is critical for maintaining genome integrity. The evolutionary arms race between TEs and their eukaryotic host organisms has driven the development of small RNA–dependent mechanisms that specifically suppress TEs while leaving non-TE regions unperturbed. In the binucleated ciliate Tetrahymena , small RNAs (sRNAs) are generated from both TE and non-TE regions of the germline genome, whereas noncoding RNAs (ncRNAs) from the TE-free somatic genome target and eliminate non-TE sRNAs, thereby selectively preserving TE-specific sRNAs for guiding TE recognition. Since sRNAs are produced from both strands, the counteracting ncRNAs must also occur bidirectionally. However, the mechanism by which the somatic genome generates ncRNAs from both strands remains unresolved. Here, we show that these ncRNAs arise from widespread cryptic transcription initiated outside canonical promoters and dependent on the developmentally specific Mediator complex–associated proteins Dima1 and Emit2. We further demonstrate that sRNA-guided recruitment of the Tetrahymena Polycomb repressive complex 2 and Dima1 occupancy are mutually reinforcing, promoting local accumulation of RNA polymerase II, which may facilitate cryptic transcription from these loci in a histone methyltransferase-independent manner. Disruption of Dima1 abolishes cryptic transcription, leads to aberrant accumulation of non-TE sRNAs, and results in erroneous genome elimination and cell death. These findings reveal a regulatory circuit involving sRNAs, Polycomb, and the Mediator-associated protein Dima1 that promotes cryptic transcription, thereby ensuring accurate TE exclusion and genome integrity.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Mediator-associated proteins and the small RNA–guided Polycomb repressive complex enhance cryptic transcription for transposon exclusion

abstract: Thermal noise communication systems transmit information by modulating thermal radiation, eliminating the need for a dedicated signal power source and making them attractive solutions for low-power sensor networks. Their efficiency enables long-lived, unobtrusive operation, which is valuable in the Internet of Things, electromagnetic interference-sensitive environments, and radio frequency identification tag systems. However, a limited understanding of the wireless channel model and efficient transmission schemes has hindered their practical deployment. Here, we present a wireless channel model that elucidates how systems operating at ambient temperature can modulate thermal noise to convey information. Our results reveal a thermal noise backscatter mechanism that enables significantly higher data rates than previously achieved. We designed and built a thermal noise communication system leveraging this mechanism to achieve data rates in the kilobits-per-second range-over two orders of magnitude higher than prior demonstrations. We also derive the system capacity and show that using polar codes, we are able to achieve this expected capacity. Our channel model and transmission scheme pave the way for strategies in thermal noise sensing and communication, advancing practical low-power networking for next-generation wireless applications.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: First-principles channel model and capacity-achieving transmission scheme in thermal noise backscatter links

abstract: Plants rely on an ancient genetic "toolkit" to establish arbuscular mycorrhizal symbiosis (AMS) with fungal partners. However, the symbiotic outcomes vary among AMS hosts, indicating divergence in downstream transcriptional reprogramming after the perception of symbiotic signals. To uncover the cross-species variation of the AMS regulatory network, we traced the evolutionary trajectory of the GRAS gene family, which encodes the major group of transcription factors in AMS regulation. Phylogenetic analysis of the GRAS family across land plants placed known symbiotic GRAS members within 12 anciently diverged lineages, with multiple lineages showing pronounced gene loss in nonmycorrhizal plants. This pattern pointed to three additional GRAS lineages as candidates for AMS regulation. Given that tomato harbors single-copy, AMS-induced genes in these lineages, we selected it for functional validation. CRISPR-Cas9 mutagenesis, combined with detailed phenotyping of fungal colonization and arbuscule morphology, and transcriptome profiling of mutant roots, confirmed that all three tomato genes are individually required for AMS development, designated Symbiosis-Required GRAS (SRG) 1 to 3. Large-scale phylogenomic analysis and protein interaction assays (by yeast two-hybrid and bimolecular fluorescence complementation) further showed that both the repertoire and interaction networks of symbiotic GRAS members vary among AMS hosts. In summary, together with 12 previously characterized lineages, the three SRGs identified in this study bring the total number of GRAS lineages with known symbiotic members across land plants to fifteen. Furthermore, our findings demonstrate that the symbiotic GRAS network has been dynamically reshaped by gene loss and rewiring of protein interactions during land plant evolution.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Evolution of the arbuscular mycorrhizal regulatory network through differential GRAS gene retention and protein interaction in land plants

abstract: The intestinal microbiota is a critical determinant of mucosal homeostasis, yet the functional contributions of Archaea—which constitute up to 10% of the anaerobic community—remain largely undefined. Here, we provide evidence that the human methanogens Methanobrevibacter smithii (MSm) and Methanosphaera stadtmanae (MSt) promote colonic health. Transcriptomic analysis of germ-free mice reveals that MSm and MSt induce distinct colonic programs important for epithelial integrity. Using gnotobiotic and antibiotic-treated specific-pathogen-free mouse models, we show that MSm and MSt reinforce the epithelial barrier, characterized by increased goblet cell expansion, mucus thickening, and enhanced epithelial regeneration. Furthermore, methanogens expand Foxp3 + regulatory T cell (T reg ) populations without inducing pro-inflammatory T H 17 responses. Notably, MSm and MSt protect against dextran sodium sulfate-induced colitis. While MSt-mediated protection requires adaptive immunity, MSm retains partial efficacy in lymphocyte-deficient mice, revealing nonredundant protective mechanisms. These findings indicate that methanogenic archaea promote mucosal integrity during host association and suggest that methanogens may hold therapeutic potential for inflammatory bowel disease, though translation to human disease remains to be established.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Methanogenic archaea Methanobrevibacter smithii and Methanosphaera stadtmanae promote mucosal homeostasis and protect from colitis

abstract: From the galaxies to the petals, spiral architectures are ubiquitous to confer hierarchical organizations, supporting asymmetric galactic evolutions and biological activities. Herein, inspired from nature, we report the superspiral architectures self-assembled by a minimalist amino acid. These superspirals, with spirality and geometry programmably tuned by enantiomeric excess and organization parameters, are determined to arise from the screw dislocation induced hierarchical crystallization. Notably, the spiral organization can integrate and amplify electrical polarization, yielding 17-fold enhancement in piezoelectric response contrast to random aggregates. This allows engineering of piezoelectric bioelectronics, resulting in high gain direction-selective motion sensing. Our work establishes an alternative paradigm for developing bioinspired hierarchical architectures of oriented and amplified properties, offering a self-assembling route to explore programmably modulated functional architectures for bioelectronic engineering.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Screw dislocation–mediated galaxy-mimicking superspiral assembly with amplified bio-piezoelectricity

abstract: The nitrogenase-like reductase CfbC/D catalyzes the six-electron reduction of the tetrapyrrole macrocycle of Ni 2+ -sirohydrochlorin a,c -diamide during the biosynthesis of coenzyme F 430 , an essential cofactor for biological methane formation and consumption. The individual dimeric protein components, CfbC 2 and CfbD 2 , form a complex to allow for electron transfer from the [4Fe:4S] cluster in CfbC 2 to the [4Fe:4S] cluster in CfbD 2 and onto the substrate. The overall process is ATP-dependent. Although CfbC/D belongs to the family of nitrogenase-like enzymes, there are several intriguing differences between CfbC/D, other nitrogenase-like enzymes and nitrogenase itself. In contrast to the other enzymes, CfbC/D exhibits a simpler molecular architecture, forming a heterotetrameric CfbC 2 D 2 assembly. Furthermore, the interaction of the CfbC and CfbD components does not depend on the presence of adenosine triphosphate (ATP). Here we report cryoelectron microscopy structures of the CfbC/D complex prepared in the absence and presence of substrates. These structures not only shed light on the molecular architecture of the CfbC/D complex but also reveal a high degree of structural flexibility within the CfbD 2 component, which undergoes a large conformational change in the presence of an ATP analog and the tetrapyrrole substrate. The interplay of CfbD with its reductase CfbC also strongly suggests an evolutionary pathway toward the modern nitrogenase from methanogenic archaea.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Conformational flexibility of the nitrogenase-like reductase CfbC/D involved in coenzyme F 430 biosynthesis

abstract: Climate change and technology diffusion will jointly drive future growth in building electricity demand. How this nonadditive response evolves over time with the pace of climate change and technology diffusion has not previously been examined, despite its importance for maintaining reliable power systems. We estimate electricity demand from residential and commercial buildings under climate change and/or technology diffusion across 183 counties in the United States through 2060. Our framework drives 209,352 machine learning models of building electricity demand with 100 spatiotemporally downscaled climate realizations across four climate models and three emissions scenarios, and 18 technology diffusion pathways of air source heat pumps and insulation. We find that the combined response of peak demand to climate change and technology diffusion diverges substantially from the sum of their individual responses, with distinct patterns across hot and cold grid regions. In cold regions, climate change and technology diffusion drive roughly up to 10 times larger peak demand growth than climate change alone by 2060. Conversely, in hot regions, technology diffusion counteracts climate-change-driven peak demand growth. Across regions, climate-change-induced warming reduces or eliminates a shift toward winter peaking driven by technology diffusion. Via uncertainty partitioning, we find climate-related uncertainty dominates near-term peak demand uncertainty, while technology-diffusion-related uncertainty increases to 10 to 80% of uncertainty by 2060. Internal variability accounts for a much larger share of climate-related uncertainty in peak demand than in temperature itself. Our results demonstrate that capturing nonadditive responses between climate change and technology diffusion is important for planning reliable power systems.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Disentangling the evolving effects of climate change and technology diffusion on building electricity demand

abstract: Obesity results from a gene by environment interaction. Understanding the impacts of environmental factors like diet on body weight/fatness has been greatly facilitated by rodent models. We previously identified the responses of males of five mouse strains fed 30 different diets. Two of these strains showed much greater weight gain and two were resistant. Sixty-six marker SNPs in 57 genes were identified, which have a genetic motif across the four strains reflecting their protection or susceptibility to high-fat diet (HFD). We used two of these strains: C57BL/6 and BALB/c, in a classic approach of cross-breeding the strains, to generate a F1 generation, and then cross-breeding their offspring to generate an F2 population. The F2 males were fed HFD and phenotyped for body weight, fat mass, and energy intake and genotyped for the 66 SNPs. Body mass gain on HFD was influenced by 17 SNPs in 11 genes explaining 87% of the individual variation in weight gain. We then measured gene expression of these 11 genes in 16 tissues of male and female C57BL/6 and Balb/c mice when fed high- or low-fat diets, and in 6 tissues of mice exposed to different levels of calorie restriction, to map their expression profiles. The genes were widely expressed in a diversity of tissues including several not normally suspected to be important for fat storage regulation (e.g., testis, lungs, and spleen) with only four expressed predominantly in the hypothalamus. Body fat regulation is probably more complex than current models focused on the brain-adipose axis suppose.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: The susceptibility to weight gain in male C57BL/6 mice fed high-fat diet is due to a small set of genes predominantly not expressed in the brain

abstract: DNA polymerase theta (Polθ) plays a pivotal role in the maintenance of stalled replication forks. However, little is known about how Polθ is recruited to the stalled forks. Here we show that PSF3, a member of GINS replicative complex, recruits Polθ to the stalled replication forks. Polθ, which is recruited by interacting with the C-terminal portion of PSF3, restarts the forks, exerts DNA double-strand break end-joining to repair the breaks resulting from collapsed forks in BRCA1/2-deficient and proficient tumor cells, and also fills single-stranded gaps on the replication fork lagging strand in BRCA1/2-deficient tumor cells. Thus, PSF3-Polθ interaction promotes the proliferation of homologous recombination-deficient and proficient tumor cells. Overall, this study highlights an important mechanism of Polθ recruitment to the stalled replication forks to maintain Polθ-dependent fork protection in tumor cells.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: PSF3 recruits Polθ to stalled replication forks to promote DNA repair

abstract: Respiratory viruses spread within the host through a combination of local expansion and occasional long-range dissemination that seeds new infection foci. We present LEAP (Lotka-Euler Airway Pathogen model), an analytically tractable within-host model that captures this two-scale process. The model takes the form of an age-dependent branching process and yields a closed-form expression for the exponential growth rate during early infection. Using empirical data to parameterize the model, we find that productive dissemination requires only a small number of successful long-range seeding events per infected cell, with distinct values for SARS-CoV-2 and influenza A virus. LEAP further predicts that, in these well-adapted viruses, interferon-mediated restriction only weakly affects exponential growth, while remaining decisive for poorly adapted pathogens. More broadly, the model provides a flexible framework for experimentally testable predictions of early infection dynamics.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Bridging spatial scales in respiratory viral infection

abstract: Precision instruments operating in harsh environments require protective materials that can dissipate impact energy while resisting heat. However, actively tunable thermomechanical protection under coupled multiphysics conditions remains challenging. Inspired by shellfish and echinoderms, here we show that an asymmetrically engineered shear-stiffening gel (SSG) yields a Janus magnetorheological elastomer whose two faces mimic the brick-and-mortar architecture of shellfish and the impact-hardening behavior of echinoderms, respectively. Unlike single-modification anti-creep strategies of SSG that degrade shear-stiffening or severely increase initial modulus, our design achieves a 40-fold mechanical tunability, with the storage modulus ranging from 11.29 to 450.28 kPa, arising from the synergistic enhancement of strain-rate-dependent stiffening and magnetic interactions. The integration of magnetic and optical functions enables semiactive noncontact 2D-to-3D protection, achieving an 85% reduction in impact force and a 40 °C temperature difference via bidirectional photothermal regulation, demonstrating competitive thermomechanical protection performance. Furthermore, this strategy establishes a magnetically guided programmable pathway for thermomechanical protection and provides a generalizable blueprint for multifunctional intelligent materials, advancing protective technologies for outdoor equipment operating in extreme environments involving coupled physical fields.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Magnetically guided programmable thermomechanical protection enabled by biomimetic asymmetric design

abstract: Urban greening is widely prioritized as a nature-based solution to mitigating intensifying heat extremes in the context of climate change, yet its long-term global efficacy remains inadequately quantified. Here we present a two-decade assessment of vegetation dynamics and associated cooling effects across 3,806 urban clusters worldwide, integrating multisource satellite observations with ground measurements from 4,855 meteorological stations. We identify a pronounced climate equity gap: While cities in the Global North have largely expanded green infrastructure, they exhibit cooling saturation with diminishing biophysical returns. Conversely, most cities in the Global South show vegetation stagnation or loss, compounding rapid warming trends. This asymmetry exposes a critical climate justice challenge, indicating that current greening efforts are insufficient to offset a warming trend. Our findings underscore the necessity for context-specific, integrated climate adaptation frameworks that address both the quantity and quality of urban vegetation to achieve equitable thermal resilience in an increasingly warm world.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Diminishing cooling returns of urban greening amid a warming climate

abstract: Plasma jets in planetary magnetosheaths are transient, high dynamic pressure structures capable of strongly perturbing downstream magnetospheres and modulating solar wind energy transfer. Although recently identified at Mars, their formation mechanisms and global occurrence remain poorly constrained. Using dual-spacecraft observations from Mars Atmosphere and Volatile EvolutioN and Tianwen-1, we show that magnetosheath jets occur throughout the Martian magnetosheath, in striking contrast to Earth where jet occurrence is strongly controlled by interplanetary magnetic field orientation and largely confined to quasi-parallel shock regions. We propose that this widespread distribution is linked to Mars' extended hydrogen corona, which generates pickup ions that drive proton-cyclotron waves upstream of the bow shock. Because this mechanism is generic to any body with an extended corona (or exosphere) embedded in a stellar wind, this finding bears on solar-wind interactions at comets and other small bodies, and on the space environments of unmagnetized terrestrial exoplanets. These results indicate that magnetosheath jet formation can be governed not only by external solar wind forcing but also by intrinsic planetary properties, pointing to a previously unrecognized pathway for solar wind-planet coupling at unmagnetized worlds.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Widespread plasma jets in the Martian magnetosheath revealed by dual-spacecraft observations

abstract: In molecular liquids such as water, time-delayed influences between microscopic or mesoscopic variables are typically probed using time-correlation functions, which are symmetric under detailed balance and therefore blind to dynamical asymmetries. Here, we characterize water's dynamics using a causal inference metric that captures asymmetric couplings between collective variables. Analyzing equilibrium molecular dynamics simulations at ambient conditions and in the high-density liquid (HDL) regime of supercooled water, we uncover pronounced asymmetries in the couplings between orientational and translational degrees of freedom across multiple time and length scales. At room temperature, rotational modes exert a modest directional influence on translational dynamics. In contrast, in the supercooled HDL regime, translational motions emerge as the primary drivers of the dynamics, suggesting facilitation-like relaxation mechanisms characteristic of glassy systems. These results reveal a qualitative reorganization of dynamical couplings across thermodynamic conditions, implying that molecular liquids at thermal equilibrium can exhibit an emergent directionality in their fluctuation couplings. As a consequence, our analysis reveals that external perturbations acting on specific degrees of freedom can induce a stronger arrow of time in the causal relations between translational and orientational modes.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Causality in liquid water as a hallmark of emergent glassy dynamics

abstract: The brain predicts action outcomes using interacting neuronal systems that integrate sensory feedback, movement, and rewards. In the mouse whisker system, we investigated whether two presumed predictive mechanisms jointly attenuate ascending tactile signals during movement. To this end, we employed an open-loop whisker-reach task that monitored facial nucleus motor activity and presented experimental tactile consequences while measuring tactile attenuation in the barrel cortex. Experimentally manipulating sensory consequences revealed two distinct systems. Sensory gating, a previously documented but functionally unclear mechanism of tactile attenuation, appeared graded but persisted during and after movement. In contrast, a second system was found to be temporally precise, generate suppression when stimuli are omitted, and capable of being learned within hundreds of trials. We label it state estimation as its characteristics-active suppression of expected tactile input-aligns well with the classical reafference principle, previously overlooked in the whisker system.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Multiple sources contribute to predictive tactile attenuation in the mouse whisker system

abstract: One of the key events in the HIV-1 life cycle is reverse transcription (RT), during which single-stranded viral RNA (ssRNA) is converted into double-stranded DNA (dsDNA). This process occurs inside the mature HIV-1 capsid and, once it reaches a critical threshold, drives capsid rupture. This uncoating is essential for infection because it releases viral genetic material into the host cell nucleus. Despite its importance, many mechanistic details of this process remain to be fully understood. To address this gap, we develop a multiscale computational method for simulating RT inside the capsid, termed Coarse-Grained Kinetic Monte Carlo (CG-KMC). CG-KMC stochastically adds deoxynucleotide triphosphates (dNTPs) to the coarse-grained RNA model, enabling stepwise growth of DNA inside the HIV-1 capsid. We implement this method within an integrative coarse-grained framework that combines a "bottom-up" capsid model with a "top-down" representation of the viral RNA/DNA genome. Our simulations phenomenologically capture and predict diverse capsid rupture pathways during RT. The resulting ruptured structures closely match previously identified cryo-ET images. We further perform an extensive analysis of the rupture process, examining its mechanistic and kinetic aspects as well as the role of capsid-DNA interactions. Our findings illuminate how different capsid-DNA conditions give rise to distinct rupture pathways, which differ from ruptures due to simple outward pressure expansion models from within the capsid.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Mechanism of HIV-1 capsid rupture and uncoating by reverse transcription

abstract: The correlation between specific amyloid fibril polymorphs and diseases suggests that characterization of heterogeneity in the aggregation process is key to understanding disease mechanisms. In this work, we use single-molecule Förster resonance energy transfer (FRET) spectroscopy and molecular dynamics (MD) simulation to quantitatively characterize dimerization of amyloid β (Aβ), the first step of the aggregation process. We find that dimerization is extremely rare, with a high dissociation constant of >16 mM, yet there are multiple dimer states with distinct FRET efficiencies and stabilities, many of which survive for milliseconds to seconds. The dimer population increases with the increasing ionic strength and decreasing pH, indicating the importance of nonspecific electrostatic interactions in dimer formation. MD simulations with enhanced sampling demonstrate the formation of diverse bound states having a range of FRET efficiencies and flexible N termini, compatible with the experimental observations. There are conformational clusters represented by the formation of three mixed parallel/antiparallel β strands forming Greek key-like motifs and the formation of antiparallel β strands, which may be representative of dimers with longer and shorter lifetimes, respectively, observed in the FRET experiment. This structural and kinetic heterogeneity, resulting from transient interactions, reflects the rugged energy landscape of amyloid formation and may be related to the great diversity of fibrils ultimately formed in the aggregation process.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Heterogeneous amyloid β dimerization revealed by single-molecule FRET and MD simulation

abstract: Bovine viral diarrhea virus (BVDV) is a major contagious pathogen of ruminants and imposes substantial economic burdens on the global livestock industry. The viral envelope glycoprotein E2 mediates host cell attachment by recognizing the CD46 receptor; however, the molecular basis of this interaction remains unclear. Here, we report the crystal structure of BVDV-1 E2 in complex with bovine CD46 at 3.1-Å resolution. The structure reveals that the SCR1-2 domains of CD46 engage the DII-DIV domains of E2 in a roughly antiparallel orientation. Atomic interactions at the E2/CD46 interface are dominated by van der Waals contacts, accompanied by only a limited number of hydrogen bonds, which explains the observed low-affinity binding between the two molecules. Structural analysis and mutagenesis studies identify key receptor features that govern host susceptibility to the virus and propose an interesting bipartite model: The D'/D interloop within SCR1 of CD46 likely serves as the "molecular determinant," and key interface residues within SCR2 function as the "affinity regulator." We further engineered CD46 decoy proteins exhibiting over 1,800-fold higher apparent binding to E2 than the wild-type receptor and demonstrated their potent virus-neutralizing activity. Collectively, these findings elucidate the molecular basis of CD46 recognition by BVDV, provide a structural framework for understanding the viral host range, and establish a receptor-based strategy for potential antiviral intervention.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Structure of bovine viral diarrhea virus E2 glycoprotein in complex with CD46 reveals the molecular basis of virus–receptor recognition

abstract: Keratan sulfate (KS) is a unique and widely distributed glycosaminoglycans family implicated in diverse biological processes. KS features branched glycan architectures with diverse sialylation and sulfation patterns, encoding a vastly expanded chemical and biological space. The limited accessibility of well-defined structures has hindered precise investigations into the KS biological functions. Here we report a programmable chemoenzymatic platform for assembling a 106-membered library of KS N -glycans and their nonsulfated counterparts, featuring length-variable oligo- N -acetyllactosamine (LacNAc) extensions and encompassing diverse sulfation and sialylation patterns. The synthetic strategy integrates length-controlled iterative glycosylation to assemble versatile precursors, orthogonal deprotection for site-specific sulfation, and modular enzyme-driven diversification. Glycan microarray analysis of this comprehensive library reveals that glycan–protein recognition is governed by the interplay of sulfation and sialylation patterns, oligo-LacNAc chain length, and terminal epitope presentation, providing insight into the functional versatility of KS glycans.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Programmable chemoenzymatic synthesis of a keratan sulfate N -glycan library for glycocode decoding

abstract: Riboswitches are noncoding RNA regulatory motifs predominantly found in bacteria. Signaling molecules such as c-di-GMP, c-di-AMP, and 3',3'-cGAMP have been reported to be recognized by riboswitches. In contrast, 2',3'-cGAMP functions as a second messenger in mammalian cells, yet its interaction with RNA molecules remains unclear. Here, we report the crystal structures of a c-di-GMP-II riboswitch variant, c-di-GMP-II-Bh, bound to 2',3'-cGAMP and 3',3'-cGAMP. Both complexes adopt a similar overall RNA scaffold with an identical binding pocket composition. However, the ligand bases adopt inverted orientations in the binding pocket, resulting in distinct interaction patterns with residues A64 and G68 and differences in base-pair stacking against the phosphodiester backbone. Structural comparison together with ligand-binding assays of structure-guided mutants using isothermal titration calorimetry reveals the molecular principles by which an RNA riboswitch discriminates among cyclic dinucleotide linkage isomers, highlighting the remarkable sensitivity of RNA binding pockets to subtle ligand structural variations and provides a mechanistic framework for understanding ligand specificity in RNA-small molecule recognition.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Molecular basis for discrimination of cGAMP linkage isomers by a c-di-GMP-II riboswitch variant

abstract: Type I interferon (IFN) signaling is a central antiviral defense, with STAT2 driving the expression of IFN-stimulated genes (ISGs) to restrict viral infection. Zika virus (ZIKV) and dengue virus evade this pathway through nonstructural protein 5 (NS5)-mediated ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation of STAT2, yet the contribution of this immune-evasion strategy to viral fitness and pathogenesis remains incompletely defined. Here, using a multistep mutational scanning strategy that jointly assessed STAT2 degradation and viral RNA replication, we identified a single NS5 residue, L162, as uniquely permissive to substitution that abolishes STAT2 degradation without compromising intrinsic replication functions. Substitution of L162 with alanine or glycine (L162A or L162G) selectively disrupted NS5 recruitment of the ZSWIM8-CUL3 E3 ubiquitin ligase, thereby preserving STAT2 stability and restoring IFN signaling. Recombinant ZIKV carrying these mutations exhibited reduced replication and enhanced ISG induction in human cells, defects fully rescued by STAT2 knockout. In A129 mice (type I IFN receptor deficient), mutant and WT viruses replicated comparably, but in human STAT2 knock-in mice, ZIKV-NS5 L162G exhibited markedly reduced viral loads and disease. In pregnant human STAT2 knock-in mice, the mutant also reduced placental and fetal viral burdens and adverse pregnancy outcomes. Notably, infection with ZIKV-NS5 L162G elicited robust neutralizing antibody and T cell responses that conferred protection against WT challenge. Together, these findings establish NS5-mediated STAT2 degradation as a central determinant of ZIKV immune-evasion, viral fitness, and pathogenesis and highlight disruption of NS5–STAT2 antagonism as a promising strategy for antiviral intervention and rational attenuation.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: A tunable immune-evasion function of Zika virus NS5 governs viral fitness and pathogenesis

abstract: Ultralight scalars arise naturally in many extensions to the Standard Model and are compelling dark matter candidates. Around spinning black holes, dense scalar clouds could form through the conversion of rotational energy into particles via black hole superradiance. Extreme-mass-ratio inspirals (EMRIs) targeted by future space-based detectors will give us unparalleled access to the environments of massive black holes, allowing us to probe the presence of scalar clouds. We consider EMRIs around a Schwarzschild black hole and show that eccentricity induces a dense sequence of resonances in the scalar fluxes near the last stable orbit. These resonances arise only in a fully relativistic treatment, as they are intrinsically tied to the splitting between the azimuthal and radial orbital frequencies in the strong-field regime. By evolving the orbits adiabatically, we show that the resulting resonant transitions substantially enhance the exchange of energy and angular momentum between the EMRI and the scalar cloud, significantly amplifying the accumulated dephasing in the gravitational waveform relative to circular motion. Our results highlight the importance of eccentricity in shaping the observational signatures of EMRIs embedded in scalar clouds.
journal: Physical Review Letters
journal_ref: Physical Review Letters
title: Resonances as signatures of scalar clouds in eccentric extreme-mass-ratio inspirals

abstract: Since the discovery of superconductivity in infinite-layer nickelates, there have been extensive efforts to unravel their electronic structure and pairing mechanism. In particular, understanding how the electronic structure evolves with doping is essential for clarifying theoretical models of superconductivity in nickelates. Here we present studies of the optical conductivity of Nd1-xSrxNiO2 thin films spanning the full phase diagram 0.025 < x < 0.30 using spectroscopic ellipsometry. The data are consistent with a two-band Drude model, which allows the decomposition of the intraband response into distinct contributions. One is from a "narrow" Drude term which we associate with electron bands, and the other a "broad" Drude term linked to the hole band with strong correlations. Increasing Sr doping leads to an expansion of the hole band spectral weight, and a corresponding reduction in the electron band, indicative of the multiband electronic structure and a doping-dependent reconstruction of the Fermi surface. Both doping and temperature-dependent optical spectra display significant spectral weight transfer from high to low energy, a hallmark of strong electronic correlations. In the superconducting state at optimal doping (x = 0.15), both electron and hole bands contribute to the superconducting condensate, signifying multiband superconductivity.
journal: Physical Review Letters
journal_ref: Physical Review Letters
title: Optical conductivity signatures of strong correlations and multiband superconductivity in infinite-layer nickelates

abstract: Fluctuational electrodynamics relies on the assumption that thermal fluctuations in distinct bodies are statistically independent. It is shown that this approximation breaks down in the extreme near-field regime, where hybridization of surface phonon-polaritons across nanometric vacuum gaps generates finite fluctuating-current cross correlations between opposite interfaces. Using a microscopic coupled-oscillator model combined with a Green-tensor formulation of the Poynting vector, the resulting correlation-induced correction to radiative heat transfer is derived. For polar materials, these correlations become significant when the hybridization energy approaches the intrinsic damping rate and can substantially modify conventional fluctuational-electrodynamics predictions at subnanometric separations.
journal: Physical Review Letters
journal_ref: Physical Review Letters
title: Breakdown of fluctuational electrodynamics in the extreme near field

abstract: Open quantum spin systems offer a previously unexplored route to realizing deconfined quantum criticality. We consider a spin-1/2 $J$-$Q_3$ chain, consisting of an antiferromagnetic (AFM) Heisenberg exchange and a competing multi-spin interaction favoring a valence-bond solid (VBS) state, with each spin component coupled to a bosonic bath. Using non-Abelian bosonization and renormalization-group (RG) analysis, combined with large-scale quantum Monte Carlo (QMC) simulations, we determine the phase diagram and the associated phase transitions of the model. We show that strong dissipation stabilizes an AFM phase for sub-Ohmic, Ohmic, and super-Ohmic baths. Continuous AFM-VBS transitions at finite dissipation are found upon increasing the multi-spin interaction in both the sub-Ohmic and Ohmic regimes. Critical properties are obtained through perturbative RG analysis and QMC simulations. In the Ohmic case, the critical point features spinon deconfinement and emergent O(4) symmetry. In the sub-Ohmic regime, the transition may also involve spinon deconfinement, provided that spinons remain deconfined in the dissipative VBS phase. In addition, in the super-Ohmic regime, we propose a transition from AFM phase to a quasi-long-range ordered phase.
journal: Physical Review Letters
journal_ref: Physical Review Letters
title: Deconfined quantum critical point in a dissipative spin-1/2 chain

abstract: We address the general problem of formulating the dynamical large deviations of non-Markovian systems in a closed form. Specifically, we consider a broad class of ``self-interacting'' jump processes whose dynamics depends on the past through a functional of a state-dependent empirical observable. Exploiting a natural separation of timescales, \newnewtext{and under the corresponding mixing conditions,} we obtain the exact (so-called ``level 2.5'') large deviation joint statistics of the empirical measure over configurations and of the empirical flux of transitions. As an application of this general framework, we derive explicit general bounds on the fluctuations of trajectory observables, generalising to the non-Markovian case both thermodynamic and kinetic uncertainty relations. We illustrate our theory with simple examples, and discuss potential applications of these results.
journal: Physical Review Letters
journal_ref: Physical Review Letters
title: Level 2.5 large deviations and uncertainty relations for non-Markov self-interacting dynamics

abstract: We establish a connection between Hardy's paradox and nonlocality sharing in sequential bipartite scenarios, where each subsystem is measured in turn by a chain of observers. We show that any correlations exhibiting a Hardy paradox in the two-input two-output scenario enable sequential violations of the CHSH inequality between arbitrarily many pairs of observers, using only projective measurements and the assistance of a small local ancilla system. Since almost all pure entangled states, with the only exception of the maximally entangled one, admit Hardy correlations, our protocol applies generically: almost all pure entangled states, if assisted by a local ancilla, allow for nonlocality sharing between arbitrarily many observer pairs using only projective measurements.
journal: Physical Review Letters
journal_ref: Physical Review Letters
title: Almost all pure entangled states enable unbounded nonlocality sharing

abstract: Nearly a century after Wigner's initial proposal, electron crystals are now a topic of intense experimental and theoretical interest. However, most proposed crystalline phases are commensurate and therefore become insulating in the presence of even weak pinning. In this work we discuss when a commensurate Wigner crystal will spontaneously self dope and develop itinerant carriers, giving rise to an incommensurate and thus metallic Wigner crystal (MWC). We develop a general criterion for the instability of the commensurate crystal which involves the competition between the charge gap at commensurability and a ``packing bias'' whose sign selects whether electron or hole doping is preferred. We then apply these insights to rhombohedral multilayer graphene, where calculations for commensurate crystals reveal instabilities towards self-doping. Carrying out self-consistent Hartree-Fock over the landscape of incommensurate crystals reveals the phase diagram, where a broad MWC phase appears directly adjacent to an insulating Wigner crystal phase. Recent observations of an island of reversed Hall conductance near a putative Wigner crystal phase in rhombohedral graphene are naturally explained by our theory.
journal: Physical Review Letters
journal_ref: Physical Review Letters
title: Crystals caught doping: Metallic Wigner crystals in rhombohedral graphene

abstract: Self-organized dynamic patterns in dense active matter are striking manifestations of non-equilibrium physics. A prominent example is the macroscopic elliptical motion observed in quasi-2D bacterial suspensions, which has lacked a physical explanation. Here, we examine a minimal linear response framework coupling bacterial swimming dynamics with fluid flow, treating long-range hydrodynamic interactions as a macroscopic communication channel. We demonstrate that microscopic swim motion, via Jeffery coupling, manifests as a ``phase-leading'' response to local shear flows. System-wide sustained oscillations, on the other hand, require both a critical bacterial density and strict geometric confinement. By analytically predicting the onset cell density and maximum film thickness, our model achieves excellent quantitative agreement with experiments, establishing a unified physical framework for self-organized periodic motion of elongated body in active fluids.
journal: Physical Review Letters
journal_ref: Physical Review Letters
title: Spontaneous oscillations and geometric cutoff in confined bacterial swarms

abstract: Quantum error correction (QEC) enables fault-tolerant quantum computation but requires operating quantum hardware at physical error rates below code-dependent thresholds, which remains challenging for current devices. We introduce syndrome resampling, a general method that increases QEC thresholds of any decoder and suppresses logical errors without additional hardware, decoding modifications, or code-specific assumptions beyond syndrome statistics. The method exploits the fact that syndromes with low probability are likely to lead to logical failure, therefore biasing syndrome averages towards most likely syndromes effectively increases logical fidelities. We establish a direct connection between the Rényi coherent information (RCI) and powers of the syndrome probability distribution, showing that resampling syndromes according to these powers combined with maximum likelihood decoding (MLD) realizes a family of optimal thresholds associated with phase transitions in the RCI. Numerical simulations of surface codes demonstrate that syndrome resampling substantially increases thresholds for both optimal and suboptimal decoders and reduces logical error rates by up to four orders of magnitude in experimentally relevant regimes. We further show that syndrome resampling can be effectively implemented from finite data and combined with decoding-based post-selection to achieve additional gains. Finally, applying the method to existing experimental QEC data yields up to two orders of magnitude reduction in logical error rates without requiring additional measurements. Our results provide a practical and decoder-agnostic route to improved logical fidelities in near-term QEC experiments.
journal: Physical Review Letters
journal_ref: Physical Review Letters
title: Syndrome resampling enhances quantum error correction thresholds
